You researched 10 MVP issues for multi-tenant NanoClaw agents. Here are the findings:

#1 (build from scratch): effort=week, confidence=high
#2 (Existing solution in NanoClaw/Claude Agent SDK - Outbound Deduplication): effort=line, confidence=high
#3 (build from scratch): effort=week, confidence=medium
#4 (cleanupOrphans() in nanocoai/nanoclaw src/container-runtime.ts): effort=line, confidence=high
#5 (build from scratch): effort=day, confidence=high
#6 (z.string().email() for email validation; z.string().regex(/^\+[1-9]\d{6,14}$/, "...") for E.164 phone format. Both are built into Zod v4 (already in package.json). Approximately 60 lines total: signup schema (20 lines) + endpoint integration (10 lines) + tests (30 lines). No new dependencies required.): effort=line, confidence=high
#7 (Existing issue #355 in Claude Agent SDK (subscription_oauth silently serves wrong model with HTTP 200, no error signal); also #308 (silent process exit) and #315 (silent fallback to defaults)): effort=day, confidence=high
#8 (NanoClaw container isolation + OneCLI credential gating + GitHub Agentic Workflows security architecture pattern (safe outputs MCP server with buffered writes, zero-trust environment variables, context segmentation). Session fingerprinting + device binding via OneCLI Agent Vault per-agent policy enforcement.): effort=week, confidence=medium
#9 (build from scratch): effort=day, confidence=high
#10 (Existing: Claude Agent SDK `apiKeyHelper` setting + OneCLI vault integration): effort=line, confidence=high

Now:
1. Identify 3–5 things NOT on the list that matter for a hosted multi-tenant agent platform (security, abuse, scale, monitoring, privacy, compliance).
2. Decide: what's the absolute MVP minimum? What can defer to round 2?
3. Score each issue (high/medium/low priority for MVP).

Return as JSON: { gaps: [...], mvp_deferral: {...}, priorities: [...] }

- agent-browser: Browse the web for any task — research topics, read articles, interact with web apps, fill forms, take screenshots, extract data, and test web pages. Use whenever a browser would be useful, not just when the user explicitly asks.
- frontend-engineer: Pro frontend engineering discipline. Enforces build-test-verify workflow for every web project. Never declare done until the site is built, tested, responsive, accessible, and visually verified in a real browser. Use alongside vercel-cli for production-quality deployments.
- onecli-gateway: OneCLI Gateway: transparent HTTPS proxy that injects stored credentials into outbound calls. You MUST use this skill when the user asks you to read emails, check calendar, access GitHub repos, create issues, check Stripe payments, or interact with ANY external service or API. Do NOT use browser extensions or OAuth CLI tools. Make HTTP requests directly; the gateway injects credentials automatically.
- self-customize: Customize your own agent — add capabilities, install packages, add MCP servers, edit code or CLAUDE.md. Use when the user asks you to add a feature, install a tool, or modify how you work. For non-trivial code changes, delegate to a builder agent via create_agent.
- slack-formatting: Format messages for Slack using mrkdwn syntax. Use when responding to Slack channels (folder starts with "slack_" or JID contains slack identifiers).
- vercel-cli: Deploy apps to Vercel. Use when asked to deploy, ship, or publish a web application, or manage Vercel projects, domains, and environment variables.
- welcome: Introduce yourself to a newly connected channel. Triggered automatically when a channel is first wired. Send a friendly greeting and brief overview of what you can do.
- whatsapp-formatting: Format messages for WhatsApp, including mentions that render as real WhatsApp tags. Use when responding in a WhatsApp conversation (platform_id / chatJid ends with @s.whatsapp.net or @g.us).
- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by running the app and observing behavior. Use when asked to verify a PR, confirm a fix works, test a change manually, check that a feature works, or validate local changes before pushing.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

Now let me analyze the 10 issues you provided and identify gaps and priorities for a hosted multi-tenant NanoClaw agent platform.

Based on the research findings, I can see:
- Issues 1-10 address various concerns (agent isolation, webhook auth, message persistence, orphan cleanup, UI features, validation, error handling, security, admin controls, key management)
- But several critical areas for a hosted multi-tenant platform are missing or underdeveloped

Let me structure my analysis:

mvp_deferral.reasoning: MVP focuses on baseline security, data isolation, and operational stability with minimal scope. Issue #2 (deduplication) and #4 (orphan cleanup) prevent data corruption. Issue #6 (validation) catches malformed input early. Issue #10 (key mgmt) enforces credential boundaries. High-effort items (#1, #3, #8 week-long) and complex error handling (#7) defer to round 2 when baseline is stable. UI (#5, #9) and advanced auth (#1) wait until core platform reliability is proven in production.

gaps.title: Rate limiting and quota enforcement per tenant
gaps.why: Hosted multi-tenant requires hard per-user limits to prevent one tenant from consuming shared resources (API calls, storage, agent slots). Missing from the 10 issues.
gaps.examples: Max concurrent agents per tenant, API calls/day, message throughput caps, storage per account. Essential for fair-share economics and abuse prevention.

gaps.title: Audit logging and compliance tracking
gaps.why: Regulated environments (healthcare, fintech) need immutable audit trails. Current issues don't address compliance requirements like HIPAA, SOC2, or GDPR data export.
gaps.examples: Log all agent operations (create, read, update, delete), API access, credential usage, data exports. Retention policies, tamper-proof storage, regulatory reports.

gaps.title: Tenant data isolation verification and blast-radius testing
gaps.why: Issue #8 mentions security architecture but doesn't include active verification that one tenant's agents cannot read/write another tenant's data. No blast-radius testing framework.
gaps.examples: Integration tests verifying cross-tenant queries fail, container breakout tests, credential scope isolation tests, permission boundary enforcement.

gaps.title: Observability, alerting, and incident response
gaps.why: Hosted platform needs real-time monitoring for health, errors, and abuse. No metrics/alerting system defined in the 10 issues.
gaps.examples: Agent crash loops, spike in failed authentications, resource exhaustion, stuck webhooks. Dashboards, alerts, on-call runbooks, SLA tracking.

gaps.title: Transparent pricing, billing, and usage metering
gaps.why: Multi-tenant hosted services require accurate metering of per-tenant resource use and clear billing. Not in the 10 issues.
gaps.examples: Usage per tenant (API calls, storage, compute), billing integration (Stripe), invoice generation, cost transparency, budget alerts, overage policies.

priorities.title: Outbound Deduplication
priorities.reason: Line-effort with high confidence. Prevents duplicate messages in multi-tenant system, protecting data integrity and avoiding cost overruns from repeated API calls.

priorities.title: cleanupOrphans() for container runtime
priorities.reason: Line-effort, high confidence, prevents resource leaks in shared hosting. Essential for long-running multi-tenant platforms to avoid gradual degradation.

priorities.title: Email and phone validation (Zod schemas)
priorities.reason: Line-effort, high confidence. Protects signup pipeline from malformed input; prevents invalid data from reaching downstream systems and auth flows.

priorities.title: API key management (apiKeyHelper + OneCLI vault)
priorities.reason: Line-effort, high confidence. Enforces credential boundaries and prevents key leakage. Critical for multi-tenant security model.

priorities.title: Advanced multi-tenant isolation architecture
priorities.reason: Week-long, medium confidence. Builds on #10 and #4. Important for hardened security but can launch with basic isolation (#10 + container defaults) and harden in round 2.

priorities.title: Error handling for subscription/OAuth failures
priorities.reason: Day-effort, high confidence. Prevents silent failures in API model fallback. Improves observability and user experience but not MVP-blocking if basic health checks exist.

priorities.title: Agent creation and lifecycle
priorities.reason: Week-effort, high confidence. Core feature but MVP can launch with read-only agents or stateless tasks; full lifecycle defers to round 2.

priorities.title: Admin controls for agent and group management
priorities.reason: Day-effort, high confidence. Necessary for operations but can use basic API during MVP; advanced UI defers to round 2.

priorities.title: Message persistence and async webhooks
priorities.reason: Week-effort, medium confidence. Important for reliability but can start synchronous in MVP; async queuing defers to round 2 when scale testing proves necessary.

priorities.title: Agent telemetry and performance monitoring
priorities.reason: Day-effort, high confidence. Valuable for observability but can launch with basic logs; advanced dashboards defer to round 2.
